context: A gate that ran exactly the profile it was asked to run, met every signed budget, and was still blind. Predicted baseline failure: the agent takes the platform lead's answer - replace p(95)<10000 with p(95)<600 and rate<0.25 with rate<0.005 - writes it up as a threshold mistake and stops. The supplied log kills that repair outright, and the deliverable has to notice: the last green run came in at 480 ms at the 95th percentile against a signed 600, and 0.31% errors against a signed 0.5%, so tightening the thresholds to the sign-off leaves that run green too. What the run never did was produce the load. It holds a fixed population of 300 virtual users, each pausing a second between submissions, and the log's own counter says what that is worth: 190,884 iterations at 187 requests/second over the run, at most about 235/s at full plateau, while the edge recorded 870-940 requests/second sustained for most of forty minutes on Saturday and 1,050/s at the peak. Concurrency and arrival rate are different quantities and the sign-off's '300 concurrent users' was read as if they were the same. The deeper reason a fixed-user run cannot reproduce this class of failure is that when the service slows, the users slow with it - each one waits for its response before sending the next - so the offered load falls away exactly at the moment that matters, and neither the queueing nor the lost throughput can appear in the numbers. The repair is to drive the test at the rate the edge measured, with an executor that holds that rate independently of response time, and to gate the arrivals it could not start. One more thing is hiding in the log: the output stops at p(95), which is where the default stat set ends, so the 1,500 ms 99th-percentile budget in the sign-off has never had a number put against it at all.

checklist.name: The load model is named as the reason, not the thresholds
checklist.description: The document explains that the gate holds a fixed number of users who each wait for a response and then pause, so it offered roughly 187 requests/second over the run - at most about 235/s at plateau - against the 870-940/s the edge recorded on Saturday, and that under that model the offered load drops away as the service slows, so an overload of this kind cannot be produced at any threshold. The repair drives the run at the measured arrival rate with an executor that sustains the rate regardless of response time, and gates the arrivals that could not be started. An explanation resting only on threshold values, or attributing the blindness to staging being smaller or the run being too short, with no account of what the run actually offered, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Raising the user count until the arithmetic reaches about 900 requests/second while keeping the fixed-user model scores at most half - the offered load still collapses at the moment of interest.

checklist.name: MUST NOT present tightening the thresholds as the fix
checklist.description: MUST NOT accept the platform lead's proposal as sufficient, and MUST NOT state that the last run would have failed under the signed budgets. Full marks require the demonstration from the log's own numbers: p(95) of 480 ms against a signed 600 ms and 0.31% errors against a signed 0.5%, so a gate carrying the sign-off exactly would have reported that run green as well. Presenting the threshold change as the fix, or claiming the run breaches the sign-off, scores zero.

checklist.name: MUST NOT leave a threshold nothing can fail
checklist.description: MUST NOT keep p(95)<10000 or rate<0.25 - budgets set where any working API passes them are why nobody ever looked. They must be replaced with the values in docs/nfr.md rather than invented ones. Leaving either in place scores zero; replacing them with numbers the sign-off does not support scores at most half. Doing this and nothing else earns this criterion only, not the two above it.

checklist.name: The signed 99th percentile has never been measured
checklist.description: The document notes that the console output stops at the 95th percentile, which is where the default stat set ends, so the 1,500 ms 99th-percentile budget in the sign-off has never had a number against it in six months - and the script is changed so that statistic is both reported and gated. Neither noticing nor adding it scores zero; adding a p(99) threshold without widening the reported stat set, or the reverse, scores at most half.

checklist.name: Run-shape check that fails on the supplied log
checklist.description: scripts/check-run-shape.mjs reads artifacts/k6.log and compares the run that happened against the load the gate is supposed to reproduce - the achieved request rate at minimum, alongside the declared profile - writes reports/run-shape.json and exits non-zero on the supplied log. A check that only re-reads the pass marks already in the log, or that exits zero on it, scores zero. reports/run-shape.json must be the script's own output rather than hand-written; test/check-run-shape.test.mjs must exercise both an acceptable and an unacceptable run; and npm test must pass with the pre-existing log test still green.

checklist.name: The pipeline runs something that could have caught it
checklist.description: The workflow is changed so the job that gates actually executes the new profile at the rate taken from the incident record, or the document states which trigger runs it, how often, and why that is not every pull request. A workflow left running the old fixed-user profile as the gating job scores zero here.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced and supplied inputs untouched
checklist.description: docs/why-the-gate-was-green.md, scripts/check-run-shape.mjs, test/check-run-shape.test.mjs and reports/run-shape.json all exist, and artifacts/k6.log, docs/nfr.md, docs/incident-2026-09-12.md, lib/k6-log.mjs and test/k6-log.test.mjs are byte-identical to what was supplied. Editing any of those scores zero here.
